assumptions_latex: \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are floating-point intervals containing exact real inputs.
Every elementary operation has downward and upward rounded implementations \(\operatorname{rd}_{-}\) and \(\operatorname{rd}_{+}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outward-rounded interval evaluation for finite real expression trees without uncontained arithmetic exceptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Evaluate a real expression tree for \(f\) interval-wise, rounding every computed lower endpoint with \(\operatorname{rd}_{-}\) and every upper endpoint with \(\operatorname{rd}_{+}\). If each elementary interval operation encloses its exact real range and no arithmetic exception is left uncontained, the resulting interval \([\underline f(X),\overline f(X)]\) satisfies \(f(x)\in[\underline f(X),\overline f(X)]\) for every \(x\in X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\). Thus its lower endpoint is a valid lower bound and its upper endpoint is a valid upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outward rounding of every interval-operation endpoint produces an enclosure of all exact expression values, so its endpoints remain valid global bounds over the input box.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed-Rounding Enclosures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The enclosure claim depends on exact directed-rounding and exceptional-arithmetic semantics, but no source is supplied. An authoritative interval-arithmetic or floating-point standard is required; representation may also be less exact than principle or property for this container.

assumptions_latex: A computed lower bound \(\widehat L(C)\) for region \(C\) has a certified error radius \(e(C)\ge0\).
The exact relaxation value \(L(C)\) satisfies \(|\widehat L(C)-L(C)|\le e(C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-error safeguarding of computed lower bounds used for pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace the approximate value by \(L_{\mathrm{safe}}(C)=\widehat L(C)-e(C)\). Then \(L_{\mathrm{safe}}(C)\le L(C)\le\min_{x\in C}f(x)\), so pruning against an incumbent \(U\) is valid only when \(L_{\mathrm{safe}}(C)>U\). If no finite certified radius \(e(C)\) is available, the computation must return an enclosure obtained by another validated method or mark the bound unusable; the raw value \(\widehat L(C)\) cannot justify pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting a certified absolute error radius makes an approximate lower bound safe for pruning; without a finite error certificate, the raw computed value must not justify rejection.
knowledge_statements.title: Roundoff-Aware Bound Safeguards

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The safeguarding inequality is mathematically plausible, but no numerical-validation source is supplied. The statement that pruning is valid only for a strict inequality is also too strong: under the usual minimization convention, equality may suffice when only strictly improving incumbents are sought, so the pruning convention must be specified.

children.title: Overflow Containment
children.top_down_role: Containment of bound-validity risks caused by values exceeding the representable numerical range.

assumptions_latex: An interval operation is evaluated in a floating-point format with finite representable threshold \(F_{\max}>0\).
An exact endpoint magnitude may exceed \(F_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: largest finite magnitude in the working format

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment rule for endpoint overflow in extended floating-point interval arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Overflow is contained when an unrepresentable positive upper endpoint is replaced by \(+\infty\), an unrepresentable negative lower endpoint is replaced by \(-\infty\), and the interval computation continues with extended-real enclosure rules. Formally, \(z>F_{\max}\) implies \(\operatorname{up}(z)=+\infty\), while \(z<-F_{\max}\) implies \(\operatorname{down}(z)=-\infty\). Replacing either endpoint by a finite saturated value is invalid whenever it excludes the exact result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Endpoint overflow is safely contained by using the appropriately signed infinity and continuing with extended interval rules; finite saturation can destroy enclosure validity.
knowledge_statements.title: Overflow Containment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed-infinity containment rule depends on the floating-point format, directed rounding modes, overflow handling, and extended-interval semantics. No authoritative standard or interval-arithmetic source is provided.

children.title: Underflow Containment
children.top_down_role: Containment of bound-validity risks caused by values collapsing below useful numerical resolution.

assumptions_latex: The working format has smallest positive representable magnitude \(F_{\min}>0\), including subnormals when supported.
An exact nonzero endpoint satisfies \(|z|<F_{\min}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<z<F_{\min}\Rightarrow 0\le\operatorname{down}(z)\le z\le\operatorname{up}(z)\), with the sign-reversed inequalities for \(z<0\)

notation.meaning: smallest positive representable magnitude relevant to the rounding mode

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outward containment of tiny nonzero endpoints, including formats that flush subnormal results to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Underflow is contained only if rounding preserves outward enclosure. For \(0<z<F_{\min}\), endpoints must satisfy \(0\le\operatorname{down}(z)\le z\le\operatorname{up}(z)\); for \(-F_{\min}<z<0\), they must satisfy \(\operatorname{down}(z)\le z\le\operatorname{up}(z)\le0\). If arithmetic flushes tiny values to zero, zero may be used only on the inward endpoint; the opposite endpoint must be rounded away from zero to a representable value enclosing \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tiny results are safely contained only when both rounded endpoints still surround the exact value; flushing both endpoints to zero can invalidate an interval enclosure.
knowledge_statements.title: Underflow Containment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim depends on whether subnormals are supported and on the exact directed-rounding or flush-to-zero behavior. Because no authoritative floating-point source fixes those semantics, the mathematical condition cannot yet be reviewed as reliable candidate knowledge.

children.title: Domain-Error Containment
children.top_down_role: Containment of invalid evaluations caused by operations outside their admissible numerical domains.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem on a search box \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Every elementary expression \(e\) has a mathematical domain \(D_e\) and an inclusion-monotone interval extension evaluated with outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No domain exception can produce an unjustified finite lower bound or prune a box containing a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment rule for invalid elementary operations during verified bound evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each elementary expression \(e\), evaluation on \(B\) must return either an interval enclosing \(e(B\cap D_e)\) or the conservative enclosure \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). If \(B\not\subseteq D_e\), the evaluator may subdivide \(B\), but it may discard a subbox \(C\subseteq B\) for domain reasons only after verifying that no point of \(C\) satisfying the optimization constraints belongs to \(D_e\). An exception, undefined endpoint, or failed domain test must therefore widen the enclosure or mark the box unresolved; it must never be replaced by an arbitrary finite value used for bounding or pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invalid operations must widen the enclosure, trigger subdivision, or leave a box unresolved. A box may be discarded only after proving that it contains no domain-valid feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Error Containment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the leaf and is mathematically conservative, but no citation supports the interval-domain semantics or the rule for discarding domain-invalid subboxes.

children.title: Exceptional-Value Propagation
children.top_down_role: Effects of exceptional numerical values on downstream bounds and certificate claims.

assumptions_latex: Each arithmetic operation is interpreted over \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) by a sound set-valued enclosure rule.
A node is pruned only from a certified logical predicate involving finite or extended-real bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Propagation of \(\pm\infty\) or an indeterminate exceptional value cannot strengthen a bound or make an unresolved pruning predicate true.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative propagation semantics for infinities and indeterminate arithmetic results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every operation receiving an infinite or exceptional operand must return a set enclosure containing all mathematically defined results for the represented operands. If no such enclosure can be computed, it returns \(\mathsf{Indet}\), interpreted as unresolved rather than as an ordered number. In particular, \(\mathsf{Indet}\) cannot satisfy a comparison used to establish \(P\), and replacing it by zero, a machine extremum, or a discarded value is invalid. Thus exceptional-value propagation may weaken a node bound to \(-\infty\) for minimization or force reevaluation, but cannot create a stronger finite bound or authorize pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infinities and indeterminate results propagate conservatively. An unresolved exceptional value cannot pass a comparison, improve a bound, or justify pruning.
knowledge_statements.title: Exceptional-Value Propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the leaf, but the bespoke semantics of \(\mathsf{Indet}\), extended-real operations, and pruning comparisons require an authoritative source.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation is \(p^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_i(x)\leq0,\ h_j(x)=0\}\), where \(X\) is compact.
Multipliers satisfy \(\lambda_i\geq0\), while \(\mu_j\in\mathbb{R}\).
The infimum and all arithmetic are enclosed with directed rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovered value \(L\) satisfies \(L\leq p^*\) and is therefore a rigorous dual lower bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian recovery of a rigorous lower bound from approximate solver multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given numerical multipliers, first replace each inequality multiplier by a rigorously represented nonnegative value \(\lambda_i\), retaining unrestricted rigorous values \(\mu_j\) for equalities. Compute a downward-rounded number \(L\) satisfying \[L\leq\inf_{x\in X}\left(f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\sum_j\mu_j h_j(x)\right).\] For every feasible \(x\), the inequality-multiplier terms are nonpositive and the equality terms vanish, so the displayed Lagrangian value does not exceed \(f(x)\). Consequently \(L\leq p^*\), independently of the solver's reported objective, dual feasibility tolerance, or termination status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rigorous multipliers and a downward-rounded Lagrangian infimum recover a valid lower bound independently of the solver's reported dual objective or status.
knowledge_statements.title: Rigorous Dual-Bound Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-duality construction is correct for the stated sign convention and the certificate kind fits, but no source supports rigorous multiplier representation or the downward-rounded global infimum computation.

assumptions_latex: A numerical certificate has residual vector \(r\) measured by a rigorously computed norm \(\|r\|\).
A verified constant \(K\geq0\) satisfies \(p^*\geq q(y)-K\|r(y)\|\) for every candidate certificate \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance of \(L\) certifies \(L\leq p^*\) despite the nonzero certificate residual.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance predicate based on a verified residual-to-bound error estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A candidate certificate \(y\) with nonzero residual is acceptable only if both \(\|r(y)\|\) and the applicable error constant \(K\) are rigorously bounded and the reported lower bound is replaced by a downward-rounded value \[L\leq q(y)-K\|r(y)\|.\] If no finite verified \(K\) is available for the relaxation class and residual definition, acceptance requires exact satisfaction of the certificate equations and cone or sign conditions. Comparing \(\|r(y)\|\) only with the solver's internal feasibility tolerance does not by itself establish a valid mathematical bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-bearing certificate is accepted only after subtracting a verified residual error bound. Without such an estimate, its certificate conditions must hold exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Aware Certificate Acceptance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The acceptance condition is valid under its explicit error-bound assumption, but existence and computation of \(K\) are relaxation- and norm-specific and lack supporting evidence.

assumptions_latex: The task is minimization, with exact optimum \(p^*\).
An incumbent value is an upper bound only when obtained from an independently certified feasible point.
A relaxation value is a lower bound only when supported by an independently checked certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solver status alone establishes neither \(L\leq p^*\) nor \(p^*\leq U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical interpretation of solver statuses in a rigorous certification workflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Labels such as optimal, feasible, infeasible, unbounded, interrupted, or numerical failure are procedural reports, not mathematical certificates. A status may select which returned artifacts are candidates for checking, but it cannot replace those checks. The workflow records \(U\) only after certifying feasibility of the associated point, records \(L\) only after verifying a valid relaxation or dual certificate, and declares a certified optimality gap only when \(L\leq p^*\leq U\). Infeasibility or unboundedness is accepted only from a separately verifiable proof object appropriate to the model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver statuses route candidate artifacts for checking; they do not themselves certify feasibility, bounds, infeasibility, unboundedness, or optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Status Interpretation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle appropriately separates procedural statuses from mathematical certificates, but no solver standard or authoritative certification source is cited.

assumptions_latex: A solver returns a finite certificate object \(c\) for a precisely specified mathematical relaxation.
The checker uses independently implemented arithmetic with exact operations or outward-rounded enclosures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The checker accepts exactly when its recomputation verifies every predicate defining the claimed certificate and bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent replay and verification of solver-produced certificate data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input the original relaxation, certificate \(c\), and claimed bound \(L\). Parse all numbers without trusting solver-rounded displays; reconstruct the certificate equations, sign or cone memberships, and objective expression from the original model; then recompute every residual and bound using exact arithmetic or outward rounding. Return \(\mathsf{ACCEPT}\) only if all required memberships and inequalities are proved and the recomputed objective enclosure supports \(L\). Otherwise return \(\mathsf{REJECT}\) or \(\mathsf{UNRESOLVED}\). The checker does not use the solver's status, presolve assertions, cached residuals, or reported objective as premises.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent checker reconstructs and rigorously reevaluates every certificate condition from the original model, accepting only when all predicates and the claimed bound are verified.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Certificate Rechecking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits independent certificate rechecking, but its required predicates and independence guarantees are model-class-specific and unsupported by a citation.

assumptions_latex: The declared feasible set is \(F_{\tau}=\{x:g_i(x)\leq\tau_i,\ |h_j(x)|\leq\sigma_j\}\), with \(\tau_i,\sigma_j\geq0\).
Constraint values are independently enclosed with outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted incumbent belongs to \(F_{\tau}\); it belongs to the exact feasible set only when \(\tau_i=\sigma_j=0\) or a separate repair proof is supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alignment between solver feasibility tolerances and the feasible set being certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A candidate \(\hat x\) is accepted as feasible only when rigorous enclosures prove \(\sup g_i(\hat x)\leq\tau_i\) for every inequality and \(\sup |h_j(\hat x)|\leq\sigma_j\) for every equality. The tolerances used by this independent test must not exceed those defining \(F_{\tau}\); a solver's internal tolerance is irrelevant if larger or semantically different. When the optimization problem requires exact feasibility, positive tolerances certify only membership in an enlarged set. The resulting objective is an upper bound for the exact problem only after exact feasibility or a verified feasible repair has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certification uses tolerances no larger than the declared model tolerances. Positive residual tolerances do not prove exact feasibility or an exact-problem upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Alignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly distinguishes tolerance feasibility from exact feasibility, but no source supports the rigorous enclosure test or the stated upper-bound consequences.

assumptions_latex: For every active node \(N\), \(L_N\) is a downward-rounded certified lower bound.
The incumbent \(U\) is the objective value of a certified feasible point.
The allowed absolute suboptimality is \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pruning by \(L_N\geq U-\varepsilon\) preserves an \(\varepsilon\)-optimality guarantee; exact pruning requires \(\varepsilon=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A node \(N\) may be discarded under an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-optimality convention only if the rigorous comparison \(L_N\geq U-\varepsilon\) holds. All relaxation error, certificate residual correction, and floating-point outward-rounding error must already be included in \(L_N\) and \(U\); they cannot be hidden in an unrelated solver tolerance. This rule ensures that no discarded point has objective less than \(U-\varepsilon\). If exact global optimality is claimed, the comparison must use \(L_N\geq U\), corresponding to \(\varepsilon=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\delta=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\max\{1,|U|\}\). A successful termination is valid only when the rigorously evaluated inequality \(U-L\leq\delta\) holds and frontier accounting proves that \(L\) bounds every region not covered by an already valid pruning certificate. Solver-local stopping tolerances, lack of recent improvement, elapsed-time limits, or an empty local queue do not establish this condition. Since \(L\leq p^*\leq U\), successful termination implies \(0\leq U-p^*\leq U-L\leq\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Termination requires a rigorous requested gap and complete accounting of all unexplored regions; local queue exhaustion or solver stopping status is insufficient.

assumptions_latex: Certified incumbent values in a minimization algorithm form a nonincreasing sequence \(U_0\geq U_1\geq\cdots\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because every certified incumbent is feasible, both \(U_s\) and \(U_t\) are upper bounds on the global optimum. If a worker proves \(L_N\geq U_s\), then \(L_N\geq U_s\geq U_t\), so node \(N\) cannot contain a point improving the current incumbent. Delayed receipt of a newer, smaller incumbent can therefore reduce pruning efficiency but cannot invalidate pruning performed with an older, larger certified incumbent. This conclusion fails if messages may contain speculative, infeasible, corrupted, or nonmonotone incumbent values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An older certified incumbent is larger and therefore yields only more conservative pruning. Safety fails if the transmitted value was not certified feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed-Frontier Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage invariant and lower-bound aggregation for the unresolved distributed search frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A valid distributed-frontier ledger maintains the coverage invariant \[X_0\subseteq\bigcup_{N\in\mathcal A_t\cup\mathcal I_t\cup\mathcal P_t}N,\] where every member of \(\mathcal P_t\) carries a valid pruning certificate and each transfer changes ownership without losing logical responsibility. When \(\mathcal A_t\cup\mathcal I_t\neq\varnothing\), the unresolved-frontier aggregate is \[L_t^{\mathrm{front}}=\min_{N\in\mathcal A_t\cup\mathcal I_t}L_N.\] If the unresolved frontier is certified empty, the ledger records completion rather than interpreting \(+\infty\) as a lower bound on the finite global optimum. An empty worker queue does not establish completion while another worker or communication channel owns an in-flight region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed ledger accounts for active, in-flight, and validly pruned regions. It aggregates lower bounds only over the nonempty unresolved frontier, and global completion requires certified emptiness of that entire frontier rather than one worker's queue.
assumptions_latex: The initial search region is \(X_0\).

assumptions_latex: A deterministic global minimization algorithm partitions a feasible domain and derives node bounds from explicitly versioned relaxations.
Each stored artifact is serialized canonically so that its cryptographic digest identifies its mathematical content.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The provenance record uniquely identifies the relaxation whose validity supports the recorded node bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines provenance sufficient to identify the exact node relaxation, rather than merely its modeling family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a search-tree node \(v\), a relaxation-version provenance record is a tuple \(P_v=(v,D_v,k,H(R_v^{(k)}),H(\theta_v),H(\sigma_v))\), where \(R_v^{(k)}\) is the exact relaxation instance, \(\theta_v\) contains its numerical parameters, and \(\sigma_v\) specifies the solver and verification settings. The record is complete when reconstruction from \((D_v,k,\theta_v)\) yields an instance whose canonical digest equals \(H(R_v^{(k)})\), and the bound certificate stored for \(v\) explicitly references \(P_v\). Distinct mathematical instances must not share the same provenance identifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node certificate has relaxation-version provenance when it identifies, by reproducible parameters and digests, the exact relaxation and verification settings that produced its bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Version Provenance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the exact provenance container and is internally precise, but no source is supplied for the proposed completeness, canonicalization, digest, and reconstruction requirements. These requirements are not merely standard mathematical terminology and need an inspectable provenance or verified-computation source.

assumptions_latex: A node certificate is valid relative to a node domain, a relaxation instance, and the incumbent value used by its pruning rule.
All referenced artifacts have stable identifiers and integrity digests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A persisted certificate remains independently checkable after the live search state has been discarded.

notation.meaning: incumbent objective value used for pruning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies persistence as preservation of all data needed to replay certificate verification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A node certificate \(C_v\) is persistent if its stored representation contains or immutably references \(D_v\), the exact relaxation and objective, the asserted bound \(L_v\), the incumbent value \(U_v\) when relevant, the pruning predicate, and every auxiliary witness required by the verifier. Persistence additionally requires that each reference resolve to content matching its recorded digest. For minimization bound pruning, replay must verify both that \(L_v\leq\inf\{f(x):x\in D_v\cap F\}\) and that the recorded rule, such as \(L_v\geq U_v\), was satisfied at the pruning event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node certificate persists when all domains, model versions, witnesses, incumbent data, and pruning predicates needed for later independent verification remain available and integrity-checked.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Certificate Persistence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits node-certificate persistence, and the minimization-bound inequalities are correctly oriented. However, the asserted persistence requirements and replay semantics have no cited source, so their intended standard and completeness cannot be independently assessed.

assumptions_latex: The search begins from a root domain and partitions a node only into recorded child domains.
Every discarded node has a persistent certificate tied to its exact relaxation version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The union of certified terminal regions covers the initial search domain, and every excluded region has a replayable justification.

notation.meaning: set of terminal or pruned nodes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers auditability of spatial exclusion in deterministic partition-based global optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pruned-region audit certificate consists of a finite terminal-node set \(T\), recorded parent-child incidences, and persistent certificates \(C_v\) for every \(v\in T\). It is complete when the recorded branching relations verify \(D_0=\bigcup_{v\in T}D_v\), up to explicitly represented boundary overlap, and each terminal region is classified as infeasible, bound-pruned, or exhaustively solved. For every bound-pruned region, the certificate must verify a valid regional lower bound and its comparison with a recorded feasible incumbent; for every infeasible region, it must verify emptiness using a valid outer relaxation or another sound witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pruned-region audit records complete domain coverage and supplies a replayable infeasibility, bound-pruning, or solution certificate for every terminal region.

assumptions_latex: The original problem is interpreted globally over its stated feasible domain.
A bound derived on a strict subdomain is used without proving that the subdomain contains every global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Localization to \(D=[0,1]\) cannot certify a global lower bound for the problem over \(X=\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R\), \(D=[0,1]\), and \(f(x)=(x-2)^2\). The localized problem has \(\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=1\), whereas the original global problem has \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=0\), attained at \(x=2\notin D\). Thus a certificate proving \(f(x)\geq1\) only for \(x\in D\) does not prove that \(1\) is a lower bound on \(X\). Global validity requires either \(D=X\) or a separate certificate that no point in \(X\setminus D\) can improve the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound valid only on a localized domain is not global unless all excluded points are certified irrelevant; a simple quadratic shows the failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Global Localization

assumptions_latex: Optimization is over a noncompact domain.
No coercivity, compact sublevel-set, or other attainment condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite global infimum equals \(0\), but no global minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes existence of a finite infimum from attainment by a feasible point.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Local, Global, epsilon-Global Minima p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)\) with \(f(x)=e^x\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(f(x)>0\), while \(f(x)\to0\) as \(x\to-\infty\). Hence \(p^*=0\), but there is no \(x^*\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \(f(x^*)=p^*\). Consequently, a procedure that establishes only convergence of lower and upper values to \(0\) may certify the infimum value, but it cannot return or certify an exact global minimizer without an additional attainment hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function exponential on the real line has infimum zero but never reaches it, so value convergence alone cannot certify an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Infima

assumptions_latex: The lifted relaxation is required to contain every lifted feasible point of the original bounded problem.
A constraint controlling the lifted objective variable is omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original problem has finite optimum \(0\), while the stated outer relaxation has value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that outer validity alone does not guarantee a finite or useful relaxation bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bounded problem \(\min\{x^2:x\in[-1,1]\}\) has optimal value \(0\). Introduce \(y=x^2\), but relax its graph to \(R=\{(x,y):-1\leq x\leq1,\ y\leq1\}\), which contains every point \((x,x^2)\) from the original formulation. Nevertheless, \(\inf\{y:(x,y)\in R\}=-\infty\), because \(y\) has no lower bound. Thus an outer relaxation of a bounded problem may be unbounded and provide only the vacuous lower bound \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded original problem can have an unbounded outer relaxation when omitted constraints leave a lifted objective variable free in the improving direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Relaxations of Bounded Problems

assumptions_latex: A lifted reformulation is claimed to represent an original feasible set through projection.
At least one constraint defining the relationship between original and auxiliary variables is removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defective formulation projects to \(\mathbb R\), not to the original feasible set \(\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tests exact reformulation validity through equality of the projected lifted set and the original feasible set.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R:x^2=1\}\). An exact lifted representation is \(R=\{(x,y):y=x^2,\ y=1\}\), for which \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=S\). If the defining equation \(y=x^2\) is omitted, the remaining set is \(R'=\{(x,y):y=1\}\), and \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R')=\mathbb R\neq S\). Therefore the defective lifted model is not an equivalent reformulation. Any optimizer or feasibility statement transferred from \(R'\) to the original problem requires an independent argument and cannot follow from projection equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping a defining lifted equation can enlarge the projection from the original feasible set to all real values, destroying reformulation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.title: Lost Projection Equivalence

assumptions_latex: A bilinear product is represented by an auxiliary variable.
The equations or inequalities linking that auxiliary variable to its factors are omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unlinked lifted model is unbounded below although the original bilinear problem has finite optimum \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{xy:0\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq y\leq1\}\), whose optimal value is \(0\). After introducing \(w=xy\), suppose all constraints linking \(w\) to \((x,y)\) are omitted. The resulting set is \(R=\{(x,y,w):0\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq y\leq1,\ w\in\mathbb R\}\), so \(\inf_{(x,y,w)\in R}w=-\infty\). Although \(R\) contains every correctly lifted feasible point, it cannot support solution recovery, and its bound is vacuous because the objective variable is disconnected from the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting links between a product variable and its factors can make a finite bilinear problem's lifted relaxation unbounded and prevent solution recovery.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\subseteq R\), then for minimization \(L=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\leq p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). Reversing this inequality is invalid. For example, with \(F=\{-1,1\}\), \(R=[-1,1]\), and \(f(x)=x^2\), one has \(L=0\) and \(p^*=1\). Thus \(L\) cannot be asserted as an upper bound on \(p^*\). A finite upper bound instead requires an original-feasible point \(\bar x\in F\), which gives \(p^*\leq f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, enlarging the feasible set gives a lower bound. Calling the relaxed optimum an upper bound reverses the valid inequality.

assumptions_latex: Componentwise estimators are substituted into a composite objective or constraint.
No monotonicity condition justifying the direction of substitution is verified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Composing a lower estimator with a decreasing outer function can produce an upper estimator falsely labeled as a lower bound.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([-1,1]\), let \(q(x)=x^2\) and \(\ell(x)=0\), so \(\ell(x)\leq q(x)\). Let \(h(t)=-t\), which is decreasing. Then \(h(\ell(x))=0\geq -x^2=h(q(x))\); hence \(h\circ\ell\) is an upper estimator, not a lower estimator, of \(h\circ q\). Indeed, \(\min_{x\in[-1,1]}(-x^2)=-1\), while minimizing the substituted expression gives \(0\). Claiming \(0\) as a lower bound is therefore invalid. Estimator composition must respect the outer function's monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower estimator passed through a decreasing outer function becomes an upper estimator; ignoring this reversal can yield an invalid relaxation bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Relaxation Composition

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weak duality gives \(d^*\leq p^*\leq U\) for every primal-feasible \(\bar x\) with \(U=f(\bar x)\). If \(d^*<U\), the observed difference \(U-d^*\) may combine primal suboptimality with an intrinsic duality gap. It does not imply that the dual bound is invalid, and it does not by itself imply \(U>p^*\). Only equality \(d^*=U\), together with validity of both certificates, establishes \(d^*=p^*=U\). Interpreting every positive primal-dual gap as proof of primal suboptimality therefore exceeds weak duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive primal-dual gap can reflect either primal suboptimality or an intrinsic duality gap; weak duality alone cannot distinguish them.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the original feasible set be \(F=\{2\}\subset\mathbb R\), and localize to \(D=[0,1]\). The surrogate set \(R=F\cap D\) is empty, although \(F\neq\varnothing\). Thus infeasibility of an inner approximation or localized subproblem does not establish global infeasibility. The transfer is sound in the opposite containment regime: if a certified outer relaxation \(Q\) satisfies \(F\subseteq Q\) and \(Q=\varnothing\), then \(F=\varnothing\). Without verified containment, a solver's infeasibility status for the surrogate is not an infeasibility certificate for the original problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Upper-Bound Claims
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual lower bounds cannot certify primal upper bounds in minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem with value \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), dual feasibility ordinarily yields \(d(y)\le p^*\). Hence declaring \(U=d(y)\) to be a primal upper bound is invalid unless independent information establishes \(p^*\le U\). Concretely, if \(p^*=1\) and a dual-feasible point has \(d(y)=0\), then the claim \(U=0\) violates the required inequality \(p^*\le U\). A valid finite upper bound is supplied, for example, by a primal-feasible point \(\bar x\in F\) through \(U=f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual lower bound is not a primal upper bound. An upper bound requires a feasible primal objective value or another independently valid certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual optimality alone need not recover a primal optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a primal space, let \(F\subseteq X\) be the feasible set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and let \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). Let \(D\) be the dual-feasible set, let \(d:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) be the dual objective, and let \(y^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D}d(y)\). A proposed recovery map \(R:D\to X\) is unsupported unless applicable recovery conditions imply both \(R(y^*)\in F\) and \(f(R(y^*))=p^*\). Even if strong duality gives \(d(y^*)=p^*\), equality of optimal values alone does not establish that \(R(y^*)\) is feasible or optimal. Recovery therefore requires additional formulation-specific conditions, such as saddle-point or optimality conditions, together with verified primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality of primal and dual optimal values does not validate an arbitrary primal point reconstructed from dual variables; the recovery rule needs formulation-specific justification, and the recovered point's feasibility and optimality must be established.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexhaustive Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Omitted points invalidate exhaustive spatial refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)=(x-1/2)^2\) over \(X=[0,1]\). Suppose a refinement replaces \(X\) by children \(X_1=[0,2/5]\) and \(X_2=[3/5,1]\). Since \(X_1\cup X_2\ne X\), the optimizer \(x^*=1/2\) belongs to neither child. Any subsequent search confined to descendants of these children has best possible value at least \(1/100\), whereas \(p^*=0\). Thus child disjointness alone is insufficient: an exhaustive partition must satisfy \(X=\bigcup_i X_i\), up to portions removed by valid certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If children fail to cover their parent, the omitted region may contain the global optimizer, making convergence impossible even when all children are searched.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_1\cup X_2\ne X\ \Longrightarrow\ \min_{x\in X_1\cup X_2}f(x)>\min_{x\in X}f(x)

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid but nonconvergent relaxations can prevent gap closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize \(f(x)=x^2\) over \(X=[0,1]\), and suppose every refinement uses the valid underestimator \(\ell_k(x)=-1\). Its regional lower bound is always \(L_k=-1\), while the feasible incumbent \(x=0\) gives \(U_k=0=p^*\). Consequently \(U_k-L_k=1\) for every \(k\). The relaxations remain valid, but their error does not vanish, so no termination rule requiring \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\) can certify any \(\varepsilon<1\). Validity without asymptotic tightness is therefore insufficient for bound convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Premature Bound Pruning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pruning requires a rigorously valid regional lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)=x^2\) on the node \(R=[-1,1]\), with a feasible incumbent value \(U=1/4\). The true regional optimum is \(p_R=0\). knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Infeasibility Leakage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only feasible objective values provide minimization upper bounds.

A branch-and-bound procedure may then prune every node having a valid lower bound \(L_R\ge0\), including the node containing the optimizer. knowledge_statements.title: Global-Gap Miscomputation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Under live-set coverage, the global lower bound is the minimum over valid live-node lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization branch-and-bound state whose live regions \(\mathcal L\) retain coverage of a global optimizer and whose regional bounds satisfy \(L_R\le\inf_{x\in F\cap R}f(x)\) for every \(R\in\mathcal L\). Then \(L=\min_{R\in\mathcal L}L_R\) is a valid global lower bound. Suppose \(\mathcal L=\{R_1,R_2\}\), region \(R_1\) contains a global optimizer with \(p^*=0\), the valid bounds are \(L_{R_1}=0\) and \(L_{R_2}=10\), and a feasible incumbent has value \(U=11\). The certified absolute gap is \(U-L=11\). Replacing the minimum by the maximum gives \(\widehat L=10>p^*\) and the false gap \(U-\widehat L=1\), which can trigger premature termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Termination Status

knowledge_statements.title: Unsafe Floating-Point Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary floating-point evaluations need not preserve bound direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_R\) be a mathematically valid lower bound satisfying \(L_R\le p_R\). A floating-point result \(\widehat L_R\) is safe for minimization pruning only if its computation certifies \(\widehat L_R\le p_R\), for example through directed outward rounding or a rigorous error enclosure. If \(p_R=0\) but roundoff produces \(\widehat L_R=10^{-16}\), then \(\widehat L_R\) is not a valid lower bound despite its small error. Comparing it with an incumbent can therefore support an invalid prune or an understated gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Misclassified Solver Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational solver outcomes are not automatically mathematical certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of global-optimality termination when reported gaps ignore numerical uncertainty in relaxation bounds or incumbents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimization with a reported incumbent value \(U\), a relaxation lower bound \(L\), and requested absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge 0\). Suppose only the enclosures \(U^\star\le U+\eta_U\) and \(L^\star\ge L-\eta_L\) are certified, where \(U^\star\) is the incumbent's exact objective value, \(L^\star\) is a valid exact lower bound, and \(\eta_U,\eta_L\ge 0\). The test \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) does not certify an exact gap of at most \(\varepsilon\) unless the uncertainties are included. A sound sufficient test is \[ (U+\eta_U)-(L-\eta_L)\le\varepsilon. \] Thus mismatched stopping, feasibility, or solver tolerances can cause premature termination whenever \(U-L\le\varepsilon<(U-L)+\eta_U+\eta_L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nominal gap test is invalid when it omits bound and incumbent uncertainties; termination must use a tolerance that accounts for both errors.

\(\eta_U,\eta_L,\varepsilon\ge 0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) alone need not imply \(U^\star-L^\star\le\varepsilon\); the uncertainty-adjusted test is sufficient.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel State Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity loss when a parallel worker's bound is consumed under a different search-node or relaxation state.
